new_statements.rule_in_words: Kutu, an East Ruvu language adjacent to Swahili, is reported to have lost lexical/grammatical tone and to share the areal Swahili-type pattern of stress on the penultimate syllable of the word. This is a comparative, group-level statement (Kutu is named explicitly only for tone loss); no first-hand description of Kutu prosody exists.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the authors flag the Swahili origin of the areal penult stress as a guess ('the evidence is not conclusive').
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level penultimate stress as an areal feature; no discussion of phrase vs word domain or citation forms for Kutu. The closest first-hand modern description is of the sister language Kami (Petzell & Aunio 2019: 'regular penultimate stress and no tonal contrast'), and Meinhof 1907 gives penult dynamic accent for Zaramo; both are different languages of the same East Ruvu cluster.
new_statements.identity_note: No source describes Kutu (kutu1263) prosody first-hand. The only explicit prosodic mention of Kutu is Philippson's comparative remark in Nurse & Hinnebusch 1993 (tone loss, p.524); the penultimate-stress remark (p.558) is about 'adjacent East Ruvu languages' as a group (East Ruvu = Zaramo, Kwere, Kutu, Kami, Doe in Nurse & Philippson's classification). First-hand penult-stress statements exist only for sister languages: Kami kami1256 (Petzell & Aunio 2019) and Zaramo zara1247 (Meinhof 1907). Zahran 2023 (Petzell's student) treats Kutu-Kwere-Zalamo as a dialect continuum and states there is no linguistic work focusing on Kutu.
